method: Blind student read: lesson read end to end as a student first, then each question solved from its blind file only (stimulus + stem/options or prompts). Solves recorded before any question file was opened. Blind files in this batch carry no misconception fields.

apush-mcq-0059.reason: Stimulus: Potosi opened 1545, richest silver source in the Spanish Empire. Only A fits: silver financed Spanish state power and tied the Americas to the global economy.

apush-mcq-0060.reason: A is wrong (labor was Indigenous, not European migrants settling the Andes); C wrong (encomienda not abolished); D wrong (silver bought Asian goods, did not end dependence). B is the best available, though 'competing European crowns' is loose phrasing — the lesson teaches silver paid for Spain's own armies.

apush-mcq-0061.reason: De Bry never visited the Americas, so details need checking, but the image still shows the mine's labor system; A overstates (not useless), B and D are false.

apush-mcq-0062.reason: Table eastbound crops: maize, potatoes, tomatoes, tobacco. Maize is B.

apush-mcq-0063.reason: Turkey was the only farm animal eastbound, so the Americas had almost no domesticated farm animals to send. B is too strong (Native peoples did raise animals, e.g. dogs, llamas — the table only shows farm animals).

apush-mcq-0064.reason: Disease moved almost entirely westbound per the table, and the one-direction disease flow is what makes the exchange unequal.

apush-mcq-0065.reason: Stem says maize reached Europe, Africa, and Asia and became a staple; A matches. B/C/D contradict the stem.

apush-mcq-0066.reason: Stimulus is a smallpox account; the demographic catastrophe was the spread of Old World diseases to peoples with no immunity.

apush-mcq-0067.reason: Account: sick unable to move, healthy could not bury the dead fast enough, whole neighborhoods ill at once — the epidemic struck so many at once that burial broke down.

apush-mcq-0068.reason: 50-90% mortality cannot be warfare alone at that scale; disease killed on a scale warfare could not reach. A and B are false; D is false.

apush-mcq-0069.reason: The Codex preserves Nahua accounts — the epidemic as the Native peoples who lived through it saw it. A/B/D are false.

apush-mcq-0070.reason: Rapid conquests need disease plus Native allies; B/C/D are false (both empires had armies and tribute systems; Portugal did not supply the expeditions).

apush-mcq-0071.reason: Replacing idols with Christian images shows conversion as a goal alongside rule. B/C/D contradict the stimulus.

apush-mcq-0072.reason: A letter to the king asking for support would stress service to crown and church. A/B/D are false.

apush-mcq-0073.reason: Goods moved both ways, but Native peoples bore epidemics and forced labor while Europeans gained most — the prosperity claim ignores the uneven costs. B/C/D are false or one-sided.

apush-mcq-0074.reason: Stem states the disagreement; B is the only option that reports it accurately. A/C/D are false.

apush-mcq-0075.reason: Europe gained foods that fed growth; the Americas lost people to disease and labor. A reverses the directions; B/C are false.

apush-mcq-0076.reason: Passage names inflation, taxes rising more than fivefold, and heavy borrowing — exactly B.

apush-mcq-0077.reason: Silver funding wars and debt rather than investment weakened Spain — the broader pattern. A/C/D are false.

apush-mcq-0078.reason: Passage: silver paid for armies and wars to hold the empire — it funded Spain's wars against European rivals. A/B/C contradict the passage.

apush-mcq-0079.reason: Stimulus describes hand work in stages by many workers at once. A/C/D contradict it.

apush-mcq-0080.reason: Native labor emptied by disease, sugar needed many workers — Spain turned to enslaved African labor first used on Atlantic island plantations. A/B/C contradict the lesson.

apush-mcq-0081.reason: Both sugar and silver were produced in the Americas and shipped to Europe. A/B/C are false (sugar was refined on site per the engraving; silver was mined by coerced Indigenous labor).

apush-mcq-0082.reason: Walled city, grid streets, temple precinct — a large, organized empire with a planned capital. B/C/D are false.

apush-mcq-0083.reason: The Inca Empire was divided by civil war over succession. A/B/D are false.

apush-mcq-0084.reason: Spain kept Inca tribute and labor systems including the mit'a — built on Indigenous systems rather than replacing them. A/B/C are false.

apush-mcq-0085.reason: Table shows collapse on Hispaniola, 50-90% mortality across the Americas, smallpox in Mexico — disease caused a demographic catastrophe. A/B/D contradict the table.

apush-mcq-0086.reason: A fall from over 1,000,000 to about 500 in fifty years needs epidemic disease striking peoples with no immunity. A/B/C do not explain the speed or scale.

apush-saq-0014.a: Maize moved from the Americas to Europe.
apush-saq-0014.b: Smallpox, measles, and influenza struck Native peoples who had no immunity, killing huge numbers — the passage says the exchange changed how many of them lived — and breaking their towns and food systems.
apush-saq-0014.c: Maize, potatoes, tomatoes, and tobacco gave Europeans new foods, changing what they ate; the extra food supported more people.

apush-saq-0015.a: The sick lay in their houses and sleeping places, unable to move or stir, while the healthy could not bury the dead fast enough; whole neighborhoods fell ill at once.
apush-saq-0015.b: With so many dead or too sick to fight, the epidemic emptied towns and broke the systems that fed and defended them, so Spanish forces faced far less resistance than an untouched empire would have offered.
apush-saq-0015.c: The account was compiled by the Franciscan friar Bernardino de Sahagun working with Nahua scholars, so it reaches us through Spanish mediation; its details should be checked against other records.

apush-saq-0016.a: The engraving shows Spanish soldiers torturing Indigenous people: a bound man lies over a fire while soldiers stand around him, and more Indigenous people are held in a wooden structure.
apush-saq-0016.b: Las Casas wrote his account to expose and denounce the cruelty of Spanish treatment of Indigenous peoples. NOTE: the stimulus does not state his purpose explicitly — this is an inference from the subject of the account, not a fact the stimulus gives.
apush-saq-0016.c: The engraving was made by Theodor de Bry in 1598, a European artist who never visited the Americas, illustrating an account rather than witnessing the events — its details may be imagined or exaggerated and need checking against other sources.

apush-saq-0017.a: Spanish silver bought Asian spices, silks, and porcelain, and it paid for the armies Spain kept in Europe.
apush-saq-0017.b: Silver flowed from the Americas into trade around the world, buying Asian goods — so American silver linked the Americas to Asia through global trade.
apush-saq-0017.c: The silver was mined by Indigenous laborers working under the mit'a draft, a forced labor system the Spanish took over from the Inca.

apush-saq-0018.a: Las Casas wrote to persuade the crown, Prince Philip of Spain, to stop the cruelty toward Indigenous peoples.
apush-saq-0018.b: By describing the peoples of Hispaniola as gentle and obedient, owning little, he makes the Spanish violence look unjustified — the Spanish fell like wolves on innocent people.
apush-saq-0018.c: His figures — about three million falling to only two hundred — are so extreme they are hard to believe as exact counts; he was writing as an advocate to persuade the crown, so his numbers may be exaggerated and should be checked against other records.

apush-saq-0019.a: The woodcut shows the Cerro de Potosi, a great silver mountain, rising over the mining town below, with the ore veins labeled on its slopes and churches and houses in the town.
apush-saq-0019.b: The mountain dominates the town and its veins are named like streets on a map, showing silver was the reason the town existed and the empire's main source of wealth.
apush-saq-0019.c: The woodcut was printed in 1553, only eight years after the mine opened in 1545, so it shows Potosi near the start of the silver boom; it cannot by itself describe the mines a century later, when the labor system and town had changed.

apush-leq-0005.thesis: The Columbian Exchange transformed life in the Americas far more profoundly than in Europe: it remade diets, populations, and labor systems on both sides, but through catastrophe in the Americas and growth in Europe.
apush-leq-0005.context: Before 1492 the Americas and Europe were separate worlds — diverse Native societies with their own farming and trade, and a Europe seeking Asian trade and fresh from the Reconquista.
evidence: Maize and potatoes from the Americas fed population growth in Europe, Africa, and Asia.
Smallpox and other Old World diseases killed 50-90% of Native peoples between 1500 and 1650.
Horses, cattle, and pigs transformed life in the Americas; the turkey was the only farm animal to go east.
Potosi silver (from 1545) funded Spain's armies and tied the Americas into a global economy.
Sugar demanded forced labor, first on Atlantic island plantations and then with enslaved African labor in the Americas.
apush-leq-0005.analysis: The Exchange changed both sides unevenly: Europe gained food and wealth while the Americas lost people to disease and forced labor — so 'transformation' meant growth on one side and collapse on the other.

apush-leq-0006.thesis: Spanish conquest changed Native American societies profoundly and largely destructively from 1492 to 1607: empires fell, populations collapsed from disease, and labor was remade into coerced systems — though Native peoples also adapted, resisted, and kept parts of their cultures.
apush-leq-0006.context: Before contact, the Americas held diverse societies, including the large Aztec and Inca empires with tribute systems and armies; Spain came fresh from the Reconquista with a mission of conversion and conquest.
evidence: Cortes took Tenochtitlan in 1521 with Tlaxcalan allies and smallpox already striking the city.
Pizarro seized Atahualpa in 1532 while the Inca Empire was divided by civil war after Huayna Capac's death.
Smallpox epidemics killed 50-90% of Native peoples; on Hispaniola the population fell from over a million to about 500 by the 1540s.
The encomienda and the mit'a draft turned Native labor into coerced mine and plantation work.
apush-leq-0006.analysis: Change was uneven: some societies were destroyed outright, while others adapted, resisted, or kept parts of their cultures — conquest was not a single uniform outcome.

student_read_notes: Irish potato famine reference ('Centuries later, Ireland depended on one potato variety... a blight became a famine') jumps to the 1840s, far outside Period 1. As a student I wondered why we are suddenly in the 1800s. Illustrative but a forward leap.
'The encomienda collapsed' reads as if the encomienda ended when disease emptied Native towns. Did it end that cleanly? Needs checking against the books.
'Middle Passage' appears in the final sentence of the sugar section with no definition and no key-term entry. A student who does not know the term gets nothing from it.
'The island machine moved across the ocean' is vivid but the mechanism (who moved it, when) is left vague.
'Taxes rose more than fivefold' is a big claim; check the books.
'Hispaniola... over one million in 1492 to about five hundred by the 1540s' — check the books.
'Huayna Capac, probably from smallpox' — appropriately hedged, fine.

SAQ 0016 part (b): the stimulus never states Las Casas's purpose; the lesson narrative never mentions Las Casas at all. The purpose must be inferred from the subject of the account. Possible fairness gap.
